query: For reported HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure, what testable hypothesis could enable Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior to be predicted more rapidly and accurately under tensile and fracture testing than with established simulations? State the hypothesized rationale, the measurable gains in predictive accuracy and efficiency, circumstances in which the hypothesis may fail, relevant supporting evidence, and a predeclared result from independent measurements that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating quantitative hierarchical microstructural descriptors into a machine learning regression model will enable faster and more accurate predictions of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior in HfNbTiVAl10 than conventional continuum or finite element simulations.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated HfNbTiVAl10 exhibiting a hierarchical heterostructure (characterized by nano‐scale precipitates, multi-scale grain boundaries, and spatially heterogeneous microstructural features).
generation.intervention: Extract and quantitatively encode features such as nanoprecipitate size, distribution, and interface characteristics from microstructural data, and incorporate these descriptors into an ML model (e.g., ensemble methods like Random Forest or gradient boosting) trained on high-fidelity simulation and experimental tensile/fracture test data.
generation.conditions: Standard laboratory tensile and fracture tests conducted at room temperature with specified strain rates and controlled processing conditions to ensure reproducible microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Hierarchical microstructural features, including the scale and spatial distribution of nano-precipitates and grain boundary/interface characteristics that mediate deformation and fracture behavior.
generation.mechanism: By including multiscale microstructural descriptors, the ML model captures the complex interactions that govern elastic and plastic deformation as well as fracture processes. This detail compensates for the averaging assumptions inherent in traditional continuum simulations and reduces prediction errors while substantially speeding up computations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventional simulations, the ML model should predict yield strength and Young’s modulus within ±15% of experimental values, and produce rapid predictions (significantly reduced computation time), thereby improving both accuracy and efficiency.
generation.baseline: Established simulation methods that do not integrate detailed hierarchical descriptors, which typically show >15% deviation from experimental yield strength and modulus values and require longer computational times.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis may fail if (a) accurate and reproducible extraction of hierarchical microstructural descriptors is not achievable, (b) the material exhibits additional phase variabilities or processing-induced defects not captured by the model, or (c) testing conditions deviate significantly from those used during model training (e.g., high-temperature or high strain-rate conditions).
generation.uncertainty: Although previous studies support the efficacy of ML models in similar alloys, the exact magnitude of improvement in predictive accuracy and speed is subject to the quality of microstructural descriptor extraction and dataset consistency. The integration may be less effective if microstructural variance due to processing cannot be adequately captured.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of standardized tensile and fracture tests on multiple as-fabricated HfNbTiVAl10 samples, concurrently characterizing the hierarchical microstructure via high-resolution microscopy. Input the extracted microstructural descriptors into the ML model to predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture characteristics. Compare the predicted values against the independent experimental measurements.
measurements: Young’s modulus determined from the elastic region of tensile curves
Yield strength obtained by the 0.2% offset method
Fracture toughness or critical crack initiation measurements
Quantitative microstructural descriptors (e.g., precipitate size, distribution, interface area)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML model’s predictions deviate by more than ±15% from the independently measured values across a statistically significant number of tests, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Our approach includes several key stages, each contributing to the development and validation of a robust predictive model. We initiated the process by compiling an extensive dataset using various databases, focusing specifically on compression data for consistency and reliability. This dataset encompasses both single-phase BCC HEAs and BCC+B2 HEAs, with recorded measurements of yield strength σYS and plastic strain εf. A critical component of our methodology is feature engineering. We identified physics-based features representing structural, elastic, electronic, and thermodynamic properties, which are fundamental to the alloy’s mechanical behavior. To enhance model performance, we employed a Genetic Algorithm (GA) for feature selection. This approach allowed us to systematically evaluate different feature subsets, identifying the most relevant features for the Random Forest Regression model. The yield strength of metallic materials can be either measured directly or predicted; the physically based prediction however is usually based on rather complicated and long calculations [,]. In the case of thousands of alloys, the use a surrogate (approximate) model is more reasonable. This model is trained on a dataset that includes known values of the calculated characteristic and a set of corresponding features. A trained surrogate model can predict the values for a characteristic set of alloys which were not used for training. In comparison with the strict calculation, the accuracy of this approach is usually lower, but the procedure is significantly easier. In this work the machine learning approach was used for creating a surrogate model for the prediction of the yield strength.

There are 370 RCCAs data points from the DFT calculation. A total of 90% of data were utilized for training, and 10% were used to test and validate the results. The three ML models used in this work are random forest (RF) regressor, gradient boosting regressor (GBR), and XGBoost (XGB) through the Scikit-learn library [], which is also used for data preparation and model assessment. The RF model is an ensemble approach consisting of many decision trees to improve prediction accuracy and reduce overfitting by averaging the trees. The samples of the training dataset may reappear in the single tree due to sampling replacement, also known as bootstrapping. GBR and XGB are multi-purpose machine learning methods that can handle both classification and regression problems. The GBR is a type of ensemble model having an iterative collection of tree models, and it is capable of learning from the previous model’s mistakes. The XGBoost [] is a powerful machine learning method that makes a quick decision by implementing boosted decision trees efficiently and effectively. decision.trend: Earlier studies in high‐entropy alloys initially relied on continuum and finite element simulations that could not resolve the multiscale effects of hierarchical heterostructures. Subsequent work—both experimental and simulation‐based—focused on elucidating how hierarchical nanoprecipitates and microstructural features contribute to strength and ductility. More recently, materials informatics approaches (e.g., supervised machine learning methods) have been applied to screen HEA compositions for desirable mechanical properties, though these models have not been explicitly designed to capture the complex interactions inherent to hierarchical microstructures like that of HfNbTiVAl10.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress in both experimental characterization and data‐driven screening, no method has yet been established that rapidly and accurately predicts tensile and fracture behavior (Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture properties) by incorporating the multiscale, hierarchical heterostructural details. Specifically, existing simulations do not efficiently integrate microstructure‐derived descriptors with rapid predictive algorithms, leaving a gap in balancing prediction speed, accuracy, and failure mode fidelity.
decision.lever: extraction and incorporation of hierarchical microstructural descriptors into a machine learning regression model
decision.why: Building on the trend of progressively integrating microstructural insights to enhance the predictive capability of simulations, the next logical step is to develop a data‐driven approach. By quantitatively encoding hierarchical features (e.g., size, distribution, and interface characteristics of nano‐scale precipitates) into a machine learning model trained on combined high‐fidelity simulation data and experimental tensile/fracture test results under standard conditions, researchers can achieve a substantial gain in both prediction speed and accuracy. This method directly addresses the performance limitation niche by targeting the gap in capturing multiscale interactions. It would be falsified decisively if independent tensile/fracture tests show, for instance, a >15% deviation in measured Young’s modulus or yield strength compared to model predictions.
